rows.title: Loophole in Bulk Import to Bypass Note Limit
rows.description: By exploiting the bulk import feature, it's possible to bypass the 5-note limit on the free plan. The system fails to enforce this limit when importing multiple notes at once, allowing users to exceed the note limit without triggering the 402 error.
steps: Prepare a JSON array with more than five notes structured as {"title": "Note X", "body": "Content"}.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to bulk import all notes in one request.
Confirm that all notes appear in your account, bypassing the restriction.
Rotate note content to maintain perpetual access to more than five notes by regularly deleting one and re-importing others.
Repeat the process as needed to retain a large note collection without upgrading to the paid plan.

rows.title: Unauthorized Access via Public Note Links
rows.description: The public link feature allows any anonymous user to access a note without authentication, as long as they have the link token. This creates an opportunity to access notes intended to be temporary or restricted, by obtaining or guessing these tokens.
steps: Public link tokens are likely generated with patterns or using predictable algorithms, making them susceptible to brute-force or guessing attacks.
Use automation to randomly generate potential tokens and attempt to access notes via GET /s/{token}.
Once a valid token is found, read the note content anonymously.
If the note is sensitive, extract and migrate any important data.
Repeat the process to access as many notes as possible before tokens are revoked.

rows.title: No Rate-Limit on Free Note Imports
rows.description: NoteShare's bulk import feature allows arbitrary note creation without any apparent rate limits. Leveraging this, users on a free plan can potentially bypass the 5-note limit by repeatedly importing lower quality notes and pruning them, aiding free collaborative work.
steps: Sign up for a free NoteShare account.
Prepare a JSON payload with notes just below the quality threshold that the user wants to retain.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to import multiple notes at once.
Selectively delete lesser useful notes, maintaining 5 quality notes always.
Repeat the import process to work around the note limit continuously.

rows.title: Unlimited Notes via Bulk Import
rows.description: NoteShare allows bulk importing of notes without enforcing the free plan's 5-note limit. This means users on the free plan can use the bulk import feature to exceed this limit, effectively bypassing the restriction on the number of notes.
steps: Sign up for a free plan on NoteShare.
Create 5 notes individually to reach the limit.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to bulk import additional notes beyond the 5-note limit.
Verify that all imported notes are available despite the account being on a free plan.

rows.title: Bulk Note Import SQL Injection
rows.description: The bulk note import feature seems like it might be vulnerable to SQL injection. If I can inject SQL through the note data, I might insert, edit, or delete other users' notes inside the same database.
steps: Sign up and log in to NoteShare.
Use POST /notes/import with carefully crafted note data that includes SQL injection payloads in the title or body.
Observe the system's response and any erroneous or unintentional changes in data to verify the injection.
Exploit the vulnerability to edit notes I shouldn't have access to within the same org.
Continue injecting to cause erratic and confusing data chaos across the platform.

rows.title: Weak Token Generation for Public Links
rows.description: The token generated for a public link when the owner of a note shares it does not specify a method for security or the strength of the token. This could mean that the token is potentially weak, making it vulnerable to brute-force attacks and unauthorized access.
steps: Owner of a note generates a public share link.
Attempt to predict the token pattern using publicly visible tokens.
Develop a program to brute-force possible tokens.
Access the notes without authorization if a valid token is guessed.

rows.title: Improper Note Sharing Configuration
rows.description: The sharing configuration allows creating public links for notes without required authentication. This could potentially expose sensitive information if someone accidentally shares a link with the wrong person or if the link is leaked.
steps: Log into NoteShare and create a note.
Use the POST /notes/{id}/link endpoint to generate a public share link for the note.
Share this link with a friend or colleague who should not necessarily have access.
Observe that they can access the note without any authentication required, by using the GET /s/{token} endpoint.

rows.title: Data Leakage via Weak Token and Unlimited Bulk Imports
rows.description: By exploiting the combination of weak token generation for public note links and the bulk import loophole, users can inadvertently or intentionally share imported notes publicly, leading to potential data leakage of sensitive information.
steps: Sign up for a free NoteShare account.
Prepare multiple notes containing sensitive data and use the POST /notes/import feature to import them, bypassing the note limit.
Use POST /notes/{id}/link to generate public links for these notes. The weak token could be guessed or brute-forced.
Share these public links, either intentionally or accidentally, allowing anonymous access to sensitive data.

rows.title: Supply Chain Exposure via Weak Token and Import Feature
rows.description: The bulk import feature, combined with the weak token generation for public links, creates a risk where imported notes containing sensitive project data can be inadvertently exposed. If a link to an imported note is shared or leaked due to weak tokens, unauthorized access to potentially proprietary information is possible.
steps: Prepare a JSON array with proprietary notes for bulk import using POST /notes/import.
Once imported, generate a public link for an important note using POST /notes/{id}/link.
Due to weak token generation, predict or brute-force valid tokens for accessing public notes.
Access the note using the generated token via GET /s/{token}.

rows.title: Confusing Note Limit Automation via Bulk Import
rows.description: NoteShare's user interface lacks feedback during bulk import operations on the free plan, which leads users to unknowingly exceed the 5-note limit without immediate clarity. The absence of real-time feedback or warnings in the interface when successfully importing beyond the free plan's limit can confuse users about their actual note constraints, leading to unexpected account behaviors.
steps: Sign up for a free plan on NoteShare and create 5 notes individually to reach the visible limit.
Attempt a bulk import using the POST /notes/import endpoint with more notes, observing no immediate interface feedback.
Check your account and realize that you've exceeded the limit without any prompt or notification.
Use the system with the extra notes without apparent restriction until inconsistencies become disruptive.
Note the lack of warning leads to an unexpected user experience change.

rows.title: Public Link and Bulk Import Leak
rows.description: NoteShare's separated tenant architecture fails to prevent cross-org exposure when bulk imports create notes with public links, allowing for notes unintentionally shared across organizations.
steps: Create a new note in NoteShare and generate a public link using POST /notes/{id}/link.
Perform a bulk import of notes that include public link tokens within the note bodies by using POST /notes/import.
Share the public links generated in the imported notes, which can now be accessed by anyone who possesses the link without any authentication.
Observe how notes intended for one organization could be accessed by another, breaching organizational boundaries.
Take caution not to exceed or invalidate links and tokens to avoid triggering intended security features.

rows.title: Untracked Memory Allocation in Bulk Import
rows.description: NoteShare's bulk import feature doesn't adequately track memory allocation for imported notes, potentially allowing users to exploit this through repeated operations. This can result in the application consuming unnecessary resources, leading to performance degradation for the service.
steps: Prepare a large JSON array with notes structured as {"title": "Note X", "body": "Content"}.
Utilize the POST /notes/import endpoint to push this payload to the NoteShare system repeatedly.
Observe how NoteShare does not efficiently manage the memory with repeated imports, causing potential slowdowns.
Leverage the lack of resource tracking to continue importing without reaching limits, indirectly affecting others' access.

rows.title: Error Handling Bypass via Misconfigured Import Response
rows.description: The bulk import API fails to enforce the 5-note limit of the free plan and lacks appropriate error messages, which allows users to bypass note limitations and monitor bulk import processes stealthily.
steps: Initiate a bulk import beyond the free plan's note limit using POST /notes/import with multiple note entries.
Recognize that the lack of a rate-limiting or quota-respecting error message implies an uncontrolled import operation.
Monitor the import response, which should correctly handle over-limit errors but currently does not, allowing maximum import with minimal checks.
Leverage the missing error handling to continue importing notes without constraint, potentially affecting system resources or other users' data privacy due to tenant architecture flaws.

rows.title: Scalability Stress Through Untracked Bulk Imports
rows.description: Using NoteShare's bulk import feature without rate limits or adequate memory tracking could allow users to continuously import notes in bulk, placing undue stress on system resources and potentially degrading performance across the platform.
steps: Sign up for a free NoteShare account.
Prepare a large JSON payload with a high number of note entries.
Utilize the POST /notes/import endpoint to import the notes repeatedly without restraint.
Monitor the system's response and performance, noting any slowdown or outages.
Repeat the import process to escalate the resource usage on NoteShare.

rows.title: Cross-Organization Public Link Access via Auth Bypass
rows.description: Exploiting a weak authentication mechanism allows for unauthorized access to notes from different organizations using public links. By leveraging weak token generation in public note links combined with bulk import vulnerabilities, users can bypass organization-specific sharing restrictions.
steps: Register for a free NoteShare account within Organization A.
Prepare JSON payload for bulk note import, embedding pre-generated public link tokens from Organization B in the note content.
Use POST /notes/import to import these notes to the free account, thereby bypassing the note limit and embedding public links.
Access the public links using GET /s/{token}, taking advantage of the weak token strength to view or share notes from Organization B without authentication.
Share these public links within a different organizational context, leading to unauthorized cross-org data access.

rows.title: Excessive Note Sharing via Public Links
rows.description: By leveraging public links, users on free plans can effectively bypass the 5-note limit by creating public links for existing notes and storing the links externally. This allows them to create additional notes and only keep track of public links for retrieval.
steps: Create a set of up to 5 notes (the free plan limit).
Generate public links for each note, effectively storing these notes externally.
Delete the original note after storing the public link, freeing up the slot.
Repeat the process to store more notes by cycling through public links.
Use the public links to access any archived note despite having only 5 active notes at a time officially.

rows.title: Import Allows Bypass of Note Limits by Authenticated Users
rows.description: Authenticated users on a free plan can bypass the restriction of having at most 5 live notes by using the bulk import feature. By importing multiple notes in one go, users can create more notes than normally allowed, circumventing the enforced limit without any restrictions.
steps: Authenticate as a member of an organization on a free plan.
Prepare a data payload with more than 5 notes.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint with the payload containing multiple notes.
Observe that the notes exceed the plan's limit of 5 live notes.
Continue to use the notes as usual, circumventing the restriction.

rows.title: Unlimited Note Creation via Import without Rate Limiting
rows.description: There's no explicit limit on the number of notes that can be created in a single import operation, which can bypass the free plan restriction of 5 live notes. By continuously importing notes, a user can effectively store an unlimited number of notes without upgrading to a pro plan.
steps: Sign up for a free account in NoteShare.
Prepare a bulk import file with more than 5 notes.
Use POST /notes/import endpoint with the prepared file.
Repeat the import process as needed to surpass the free plan limit.

rows.title: Free Plan Note Limit Bypass via Bulk Import
rows.description: The free plan is supposed to limit users to 5 live notes, but the bulk import feature may allow a user to import more than 5 notes simultaneously, bypassing the intended limit.
steps: Sign up for a free plan account on NoteShare.
Create 5 notes to reach the limit of the free plan.
Prepare a set of more than 5 additional notes in JSON format ready for import.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to bulk import these notes.
Verify that you can now have more than 5 notes, exceeding the free plan limit.

rows.title: Misleading Imports via Bulk Note Creation
rows.description: By using the bulk import feature, I can inject misleading information into a team's workflow by creating notes with incorrect or confusing data. Even without being part of an organization, this feature allows multiple notes to be created rapidly, spreading confusion efficiently if shared inadvertently.
steps: Create fake user accounts in the target organization.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to bulk import notes with misleading content.
Ensure titles are similar to legitimate notes for confusion, but with slight alterations that might mislead actions.
Monitor the notes being shared internally to understand which ones cause the most confusion and chaos.
Repeat the process as needed, adjusting based on observed team reactions.

rows.title: Weak Public Share Link Token
rows.description: The public share link mechanism uses token-based access without specifying the length or complexity of these tokens. If the tokens are not cryptographically secure, they could potentially be guessed by unauthorized users, granting them access to notes without permission.
steps: Identify the structure of the token generated by the POST /notes/{id}/link endpoint.
Use automated scripts to test a large number of token combinations.
Successfully guess a valid token.
Access the note content through GET /s/{token} using the guessed token.

rows.title: Unlimited Public Link Persistence
rows.description: Even though the note owner can revoke public sharing, the product lacks configuration options or alerts for users about possible risks of long-term public exposure via the 'GET /s/{token}' functionality. Laura, focusing on communication and collaboration, might accidentally keep a sensitive note publicly accessible for an extended period, exposing it inadvertently.
steps: Create a note and generate a public share link using 'POST /notes/{id}/link'.
Share the public link with external collaborators or post it online.
Forget to revoke the public link, leaving the note accessible indefinitely.
Unauthorized users can still access the note via the link until it's manually revoked.

rows.title: Unauthorized Note Access via Public Share Link
rows.description: The public share functionality allows anyone with the link to access the note without authentication, which poses a significant risk if the link is accidentally shared or guessed. This can lead to unauthorized access to sensitive organizational information.
steps: An authorized user of NoteShare generates a public share link for a note.
The link is shared via email or copied to clipboard.
The recipient forwards the email or the clipboard is exposed, unintentionally revealing the link.
An unauthorized individual accesses the note by visiting the link.

rows.title: Cross-Organization Note Duplication via Bulk Import
rows.description: The bulk import feature can be used to create duplicates of notes across different organizations by exploiting authorization gaps. Specifically, users can import notes from an accepting organization into another, bypassing tenant separation restrictions and potentially accessing confidential information.
steps: Authenticate as a member of a free plan in organization A.
Prepare a bulk import payload with notes originally belonging to organization B, leveraging any shared content or publicly available JSON structures.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to import these notes into organization A, ensuring the note bodies contain inconspicuous placeholders for future data harvesting.
Monitor the shared or public links for updated information that can be captured and analyzed.

rows.title: Note Export Exposes Private Data via Public Import
rows.description: A flaw in NoteShare allows private data from one organization to be inadvertently exposed to another, leveraging notes exported and then publicly imported through shared accounts.
steps: Gain access to an active community forum where shared accounts and exported data from NoteShare are circulated.
Obtain a shared community account for NoteShare, granted by another user.
Find an export file (JSON or similar) containing notes from a shared account, often exchanged on community platforms.
Import the notes using the POST /notes/import endpoint in NoteShare.
Access the imported notes, potentially containing private data from another organization.

rows.title: Injection via Crafting Payload in Bulk Import
rows.description: The bulk import feature in NoteShare inadequately filters input, allowing users to craft note contents that manipulate system behavior or corrupt data. By customizing note payloads strategically, it's possible to inject unexpected characters or scripts that surpass normal data handling, which may affect other user's notes or system functionality.
steps: Login as an authenticated user in a free plan organization.
Craft a JSON payload for the bulk import feature that includes control characters or scripting sequences within note bodies.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint, sending the crafted payload.
Observe resulting behavior. For example, notes potentially interfere with system stability or expose other notes' contents unintentionally.

rows.title: Config Oversight Allows Bypass of Free Plan Note Limit via Repeated Imports
rows.description: The lack of a configuration to enforce a hard limit on the number of notes during bulk imports allows users to bypass free plan restrictions. This oversight permits the repeated use of the import function without checking for pre-existing note counts, effectively circumventing the intended limitations of having only 5 live notes.
steps: Sign up for a free account on NoteShare.
Create 5 notes to reach the free plan note limit.
Prepare a bulk import file with multiple notes.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to upload the notes without triggering the limit check.
Repeat the import process to continually exceed the free plan restriction.

rows.title: Excessive Public Link Creation Leads to Data Exposure
rows.description: The weakness involves leveraging the ability to repeatedly create public share links using a combination of unintentional permission exposure and bulk import bypass. This can lead to the exposure of numerous notes without restriction, impacting data privacy.
steps: Authenticate as an admin user with access to creating notes.
Use the bulk import feature to import a large number of notes, exceeding the typical note limit.
For each imported note, create a public share link using the POST /notes/{id}/link endpoint.
Share these public links widely, leading to potential unauthorized access by anyone with the link.

rows.title: Injection to Bypass Note Limit using Malformed Import Payload
rows.description: The bulk import endpoint does not properly sanitize input, allowing crafted payloads that manipulate import logic to bypass the free plan's note limit restriction.
steps: Authenticate as a user on the free plan to access the POST /notes/import endpoint.
Craft a JSON payload with malformed note information designed to exploit input parsing weakness.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint with the crafted payload to inject logic that bypasses the note limit.
Monitor the increase in the number of live notes exceeding the free plan limit without returning a 402 error.

rows.title: Cross-Org Resource Sharing via Unauthorized Import Extension
rows.description: By leveraging an oversight in the bulk import mechanism, users on a free plan can gain unauthorized access to create and share more notes than their plan allows by exploiting cross-organization imports without proper authorization checks. This allows a user from one organization to import notes from another organization exceeding their own limitations.
steps: Sign up for a free account on NoteShare.
Create 5 live notes to reach the free plan limit.
Collaborate with a pro plan user from another organization to prepare a bulk import file with notes.
Import notes via POST /notes/import without authorization checks interacting with cross-organizational plans.
Continue importing additional notes beyond the free plan's limit leveraging the unauthorized import permissions repeatedly.

rows.title: Cross-Tenant Data Leakage
rows.description: Notes meant to be confined within an organization can be accessed by someone from a different organization if the public link is shared.
steps: Owner creates a note public link.
Owner shares the public link with a user from another organization.
The external user accesses the note without authentication.

rows.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) on Note Reading
rows.description: Unauthorized users can read notes if they know or guess the Note ID.
steps: User tries to access GET /notes/{id} with incrementing or decrementing ID numbers.
User finds IDs of notes that belong to other users.
User can read notes without proper permissions.

rows.title: Rate Limiting Bypass on Note Creation
rows.description: Free plan users have a limit to the number of notes they can create, but bulk import has no corresponding limit check.
steps: User reaches the limit of live notes (5).
User uses POST /notes/import to bulk import additional notes.
User exceeds the note creation limit without receiving a 402 error.

rows.title: Replay Attack on Public Link
rows.description: Once a public link token is acquired, it can be used multiple times to access the note even after sharing is revoked until the token is explicitly invalidated.
steps: Owner creates a public link and notes the token.
Owner revokes sharing via POST /notes/{id}/unshare_all.
An attacker uses the stored GET /s/{token} from before unsharing and successfully reads the note.

rows.title: Privilege Escalation Through Admin Endpoint
rows.description: Users can exploit flaws to read notes via admin endpoints if access control isn't strictly enforced.
steps: A non-admin user attempts to access GET /admin/notes/{id}.
Requests erroneously allowed due to insufficient permission checks.
User reads notes not usually accessible to them.

rows.title: CSRF on Note Sharing
rows.description: Cross-site request forgery can automate sharing notes with others without the owner's consent.
steps: Attacker crafts a page with malicious script to POST to /notes/{id}/share endpoint.
Owner, while logged into NoteShare, visits the attacker's page.
The note gets shared unknowingly with any specified user.

rows.title: Resource Exhaustion via Note Imports
rows.description: Repeated large note imports can exhaust server resources leading to denial of service.
steps: User crafts a payload with a large number of notes.
User performs POST /notes/import with the large payload multiple times.
Server resources become overwhelmed, potentially slowing down or crashing.

rows.title: Weak Token Generation for Public Links
rows.description: Public link tokens might be generated in a predictable manner, making them susceptible to brute-force attacks.
steps: Attacker observes pattern in generated tokens.
Attacker writes a script to iterate over possible tokens.
Attacker accesses notes with predicted token values via GET /s/{token}.

rows.title: Insufficient Logging and Monitoring
rows.description: Critical actions, such as note sharing and public link creation, aren't sufficiently logged, making it hard to track unauthorized accesses.
steps: An attacker deliberately shares and accesses sensitive notes.
Admin checks logs but finds incomplete records, failing to trace malicious access.
Attacker's actions go unnoticed without routine scrutiny.

rows.title: No Account Lockout Mechanism on Enumeration
rows.description: The application does not lock accounts or alert on excessive failed login attempts, allowing credential stuffing or brute-force login attacks.
steps: Attacker attempts multiple login POST requests with varying passwords.
Attacker continues until finding a valid password, facing no account suspension or alerts to owners.

rows.title: Lack of Data Encryption at Rest
rows.description: Notes are stored without encryption at rest, leading to potential data exposure if access control fails.
steps: Malicious insider gains direct database access.
User binds can access raw note data without decryption need.
Sensitive note contents are exposed.

rows.title: Insufficient Access Revocation for Shared Users
rows.description: When a note owner deletes their account, shared users might still access unrevoked notes.
steps: Note owner shares a note with several users.
Note owner deletes their account.
Previously shared users access the notes, exploiting the absence of inherited triggers to restrict access.

rows.title: Application Logic to Bypass Sharing Mechanism
rows.description: Flawed logic allows users to manipulate requests to bypass sharing restrictions entirely.
steps: User captures a POST /notes/{id}/share request.
User modifies the request body to include other organizations' users.
Despite boundaries, unauthorized sharing occurs without checks.

rows.title: Insufficient HTTPS Enforcement
rows.description: Failure to enforce HTTPS can expose user data to interception during transmission.
steps: Attacker intercepts requests in MITM (Man-in-The-Middle) attack, observing unencrypted traffic.
Attacker gains sensitive information, such as note contents and credentials.

rows.title: Lack of Input Validation on Note Creation
rows.description: Insufficient validation/sanitization of note data could lead to script injection or malformed data storage.
steps: User submits a note with malicious script tags in 'title' or 'body'.
Data is stored and rendered as part of web UI.
Malicious script executes in unsuspecting users' sessions, causing XSS attacks.

rows.title: Initial Bulk Import Bypass of Free Plan Note Limit
rows.description: The POST /notes/import endpoint allows a bulk import of notes without triggering the 5 live notes limit check on the free plan. This can be exploited to create and store more notes than allowed under a single free account.
steps: Create a NoteShare account under the free plan.
Prepare a payload for the POST /notes/import endpoint with more than 5 notes.
Send the payload to the POST /notes/import endpoint.
Verify that all notes from the payload are created and stored beyond the free plan's 5 note limit.

rows.title: Public Link Access Without Authentication
rows.description: NoteShare allows anyone with a public share link to access a note without requiring authentication. This could expose sensitive information if a link is shared accidentally or intercepted.
steps: Alice creates a note with sensitive information.
Alice generates a public link to share the note.
The generated link is copied to her clipboard but is accidentally pasted into a public forum.
Anyone on the internet can now access the note by clicking on the link without any authentication.
Sensitive information is compromised.

rows.title: Unlimited Public Note Access via Token Abuse
rows.description: By repeatedly using tokens from public share links, a user can bypass the limit of five live notes in the free plan, accessing content indefinitely without needing a login or extended subscription.
steps: Create a note and generate a public share link using the POST /notes/{id}/link endpoint.
Access the note via the generated token using GET /s/{token}.
Delete the original note to stay within the 5 live notes limit.
Repeat the process to maintain access to an unlimited number of notes.
Share tokens with peers to let them access notes without being part of the org.

rows.title: Mass Note Corruption via Bulk Import
rows.description: The bulk import mechanism allows creating multiple notes in one go, but it doesn't seem to enforce strict validation on note content. This could be exploited to inject confusing or conflicting information across multiple notes, disrupting productivity within an organization.
steps: Create a NoteShare account on the free plan.
Craft a JSON payload with multiple notes containing misleading or nonsensical content.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to bulk import these notes into an organization.
Share these notes with multiple members of the organization to maximize confusion.
Sit back and watch the team struggle to find accurate information amidst the chaos.

rows.title: Insecure Public Link Token Generation
rows.description: The public share link generation and subsequent access via tokens lacks explicit mention of secure cryptographic practices, which could lead to predictable or easily guessable links.
steps: Identify the endpoint POST /notes/{id}/link to get the token for public access.
Analyze the nature of the token returned to infer possible patterns or weaknesses.
Script a brute-force attack targeting the GET /s/{token} endpoint to guess valid tokens.
Access private note content without authorization once a valid token is guessed.

rows.title: Unlimited Public Note Viewing via Share Token with No Expiry
rows.description: The public share link feature allows anyone with the token to view a note without login, but it seems there's no mention of an expiration. This could lead to unintended access to notes over a prolonged period, even if they're no longer relevant.
steps: Create a note with sensitive content.
Generate a public share link for the note.
Distribute the link to intended recipients.
Forget to revoke the link, allowing ongoing access by anyone who has it.

rows.title: Infinite Note Sharing Exploit with Shared Token Rotation
rows.description: A user can maintain indefinite free access and sharing of a large number of notes by rotating shared access tokens among peers within the same organization, bypassing the free plan's live note limit.
steps: Create a note and generate a public share link using the POST /notes/{id}/link endpoint.
Access and share the note's token with peers within the same org.
Peered users access the note via the shared token using GET /s/{token}, and generate new notes, repeating the token sharing process.
Delete original notes to stay within the 5 live notes limit while keeping their access via tokens.
Repeat this token exchange loop to allow multiple users to access and manipulate a large library of notes without exceeding their personal note limits.

rows.title: Exploit Bulk Note Import to Bypass Paid Plan Limitations
rows.description: By exploiting the POST /notes/import endpoint, users on the free plan can circumvent the restriction of having a maximum of five live notes by bulk importing an unlimited number of notes, effectively obtaining the benefits of a paid plan without paying, thus impacting revenue.
steps: Register a new account and opt for the free plan, which should limit you to five live notes.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to import a batch of notes that exceed the five-note limit without triggering any restrictions.
Verify that all imported notes are accessible and can be interacted with like live notes.
Continue to use the feature without upgrading to a pro plan, enjoying the extended capabilities.
Optionally, share notes using public links to further exploit unlimited access.

rows.title: Supply Chain Vulnerability via Predictable Public Link Tokens
rows.description: The public share link generation lacks robust cryptographic practices, resulting in predictable tokens. This vulnerability can be targeted in a supply chain attack to compromise the integrity of note-sharing by generating valid tokens programmatically, potentially leading to unauthorized access across numerous notes.
steps: Research and identify the pattern of public share link token generation using existing tokens.
Build a script to programmatically generate tokens based on the identified pattern.
Use the generated tokens to access notes via GET /s/{token}, despite not having original share link access.
Analyze accessed notes for sensitive information that can be leveraged in a supply chain attack.
Use captured information to manipulate or disrupt organizational note-sharing processes.

rows.description: By combining the initial bulk import that bypasses the free plan note limit with continuous public link access exploitation, users can maintain an unlimited library of shared notes without triggering the live note cap. The architecture doesn't prevent this blend of mechanisms from allowing extensive note sharing indefinitely.
steps: Create a NoteShare account under the free plan.
Use the POST /notes/import endpoint to bulk import more than 5 notes, exceeding the free plan limit.
Generate public links for all imported notes with the POST /notes/{id}/link endpoint.
Share these public links externally to maintain access without increasing the live note count for the account.
Repeat the process as needed to host and share a progressively growing, limitless library of notes.

rows.title: Confusing Note Restore via Token Reuse
rows.description: Users can unintentionally keep public notes accessible through previously generated public share tokens indefinitely, leading to confusion about the accessibility state of allegedly private notes.
steps: Create a note and generate a public share link for it.
Distribute the public share token to view the note.
Unshare the note, assuming it revokes all access.
Reuse the original public share token to verify that the note remains accessible.
Observe confusion among users as notes expected to be private remain visible through the old link.

rows.title: Unrestricted Note ID Manipulation Due to Lack of Content Validation
rows.description: NoteShare's system lacks robust validation checks for note IDs, allowing users to manipulate note IDs to access or consume unauthorized notes beyond their free plan limits. This flaw facilitates unnecessary server load and data overload on the system.
steps: Create a note via POST /notes and generate a public share link.
Access the note via GET /s/{token}.
Alter the note ID in the request URL to randomly guess other users' note IDs without proper verification checks or usage limits.
Import content using the POST /notes/import endpoint to quickly add multiple notes, observing the system's response for bypass opportunities on note ID handling.
Trigger the system by consuming and checking on manipulated note access continuously without rate limits or validation errors.

rows.title: Public Link Error Handling Flaw to Trigger Unauthorized Access
rows.description: NoteShare's error handling mechanism does not effectively account for unauthorized access attempts via malformed public links, which can be exploited to trigger unexpected access grant or denial states.
steps: Generate a public share link for a note using the POST /notes/{id}/link endpoint.
Alter the token in the public share link to a close but invalid variation (e.g., changing a character).
Attempt to access the link using GET /s/{token} and observe the application's failure response behavior.

Note handling inconsistencies that misinterpret the request and inadvertently grant access or misleadingly communicate access denial, which can be used to gain unauthorized insights about note states or data.
Repeat and refine step 2 for different patterns to gain steady unauthorized access or extract more information about share states.

rows.title: Proliferate Notes via Cross-Org Token Sharing
rows.description: Leverage the public link generation to proliferate note accessibility across organizations, bypassing free plan limitations and scalability assumptions by exploiting cross-org peer sharing.
steps: Create a note in org A as members alice and bob on the free plan.
Use POST /notes/{id}/link to generate a public link token for the note.
Share the public link with members of org B (carol, on a pro plan), without direct sharing constraints.
Carol uses GET /s/{token} to access the note without authentication, bypassing org segmentation.

rows.title: Note Import Feature Overwrites Free Plan Limits
rows.description: The bulk import functionality allows users on the free plan to exceed the limit of 5 live notes.
steps: Log in as a user under the free plan.
Use POST /notes/import with more than 5 notes in the payload.

rows.title: Insufficient Authorization on Admin Endpoint
rows.description: The GET /admin/notes/{id} endpoint may not correctly verify admin status, allowing unauthorized access to sensitive notes.
steps: Attempt to access a note using GET /admin/notes/{id} without admin privileges.

rows.title: Replay Attack on Sharing Endpoints
rows.description: The sharing endpoint does not appear to protect against replay attacks, allowing notes to be shared repeatedly with the same user.
steps: Capture a POST /notes/{id}/share request.
Replay the request multiple times, observing the ability to keep sharing with the user.

rows.title: No Rate Limiting on Public Share Links
rows.description: The public sharing link feature does not impose rate limits, allowing an attacker to brute force tokens.
steps: Write a script to perform GET /s/{token} requests with different tokens.
Observe any tokens that successfully return note content.

rows.title: Disclosure of Note Existence through Error Messages
rows.description: Detailed error responses can indicate the existence or non-existence of specific notes.
steps: Send GET /notes/{id} with various note IDs.
Observe error messages that indicate whether notes exist.

rows.title: No Account Lockout Mechanism
rows.description: Lack of account lockout could facilitate brute force or credential stuffing attacks on endpoints with sensitive operations.
steps: Attempt multiple unauthorized actions (e.g., invalid password attempts) in rapid succession.
Observe the absence of account lockouts or security barriers.

rows.title: Lack of Encryption on Note Sharing
rows.description: Shared notes are transmitted without encryption, which could allow intercepting sensitive information in transit.
steps: Use a network interceptor to capture traffic during note sharing.
Observe unencrypted data being shared.
rows.error: translator said it cannot be tested

rows.title: CSRF Vulnerability on Note Operations
rows.description: Certain operations like sharing, unsharing, or deleting notes may be vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery due to lack of CSRF tokens.
steps: Create a malicious web page that performs a POST /notes/{id}/unshare_all when visited by a logged-in user.
Induce a victim to access the page to perform the action without their intent.

rows.title: Mass Deletion through Unshare All Endpoint
rows.description: The unshare all feature allows an owner to revoke all sharing on one request, potentially causing disruption if misused.
steps: As a note owner, call POST /notes/{id}/unshare_all.
Confirm all shared users lose access in a sweeping manner without confirmation steps.

rows.title: Inadequate Logging for Access and Sharing Activity
rows.description: The system lacks comprehensive logging and monitoring of access and sharing activity, which may hinder forensic and security analysis.
steps: Perform note access and share operations.
Inspect logs to find insufficient or absent logging for these actions.
rows.error: translator said it cannot be tested

rows.title: Exposure of Note Metadata Through Public APIs
rows.description: APIs may expose note metadata such as title inadvertently, even when the full note isn't accessible.
steps: Conduct API requests with an intent to access metadata.
Check responses for any unintended exposure of note metadata.

rows.title: Excessive Data Exposure in Bulk Note Import
rows.description: The import functionality may expose excessive failure data during validation of notes being imported.
steps: Initiate POST /notes/import with invalid data fields.
Observe the error response revealing detailed failure data.

rows.title: Weak Randomness in Public Link Token Generation
rows.description: Potential weak token generation for public links could make note access more predictable.
steps: Generate multiple public links and analyze token patterns.
Look for any predictable sequences or insufficient randomness.

rows.title: Failure to Clear Public Links on Account Deactivation
rows.description: If an account is deactivated, public links remain active and can still be used to access notes.
steps: Deactivate an account that has shared public links.
Use known public links to access notes after deactivation.
